title: Microstructure and tensile properties of high-Si ferritic/martensitic steel thin-walled tube during the cold rolling and annealing
abstract: In this study, a high-Si ferritic/martensitic (F/M) steel thin-walled tube (T-Φ5) with an outer diameter of 5 mm and wall thickness of 0.5 mm were fabricated via Pilger cold rolling and intermediate annealing technology. The evolution of microstructure and texture during the process was characterized by various methods. Cold rolling induced the formation of typical α-fiber (<110>//AD) and γ-fiber (<111>//RD) textures in the tube. The subgrained microstructure formed after cold deformation underwent recrystallization during intermediate annealing at 800 ℃, resulting in reduced texture intensity in the recrystallized grains compared to the cold-rolled grains. The T-Φ5 tube subjected to final normalizing and tempering treatments exhibited low texture intensity and a fully martensitic lath microstructure. The average sizes of M23C6 carbides and MX precipitates in the tube are 162.1 ± 59.7 nm and 42.8 ± 25.0 nm. The ultimate tensile strength and yield strength of T-Φ5 at room temperature are 815 MPa and 686 MPa, which decrease to 279 MPa and 247 MPa with increasing test temperature to 650 ℃. The total elongation shows a trend of “initial decrease followed by increase”, with a minimum value (17.5%) appearing at 400 ℃ dominated by dynamic strain aging (DSA) mechanism. The ln(dσ/dε) vs. lnσ curves obtained during tensile test reveal a significant temperature dependence in the strain hardening behavior of the tube, mainly due to the influence of DSA at medium temperatures and dislocation recovery/annihilation mechanisms at high temperatures. This work has a positive role for optimizing the processing and practical application of high-Si F/M steel cladding tubes.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Lead-cooled fast reactor (LFR) is an important direction for future nuclear energy development due to its inherent advantages such as high safety and large power density  [1–3] . Liquid lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE) coolant used in LFR has the advantages of low neutron capture cross section, high heat transfer efficiency, excellent chemical inertness, and high boiling point  [4,5] . Ferritic/martensitic (F/M) steels have become one of the candidate structural materials for fuel cladding due to their high thermal conductivity, low thermal expansion coefficient, low thermal fatigue sensitivity, and excellent irradiation swelling resistance  [4,6–9] . However, the compatibility between F/M steels and liquid LBE is one of the major challenges restricting the application of LFR  [4,6,10,11] .

The corrosion performance of F/M steels in LBE has been widely reported. Shi et al.  [12]  exposed T91 steel to liquid LBE saturated by oxygen (∼2 × 10 -3  wt% oxygen content) at 600 ℃ for 1000 h. A four-layer oxide scale consisting of inner oxidation zone, Fe-Cr spinel, magnetite, and porous plumboferrite was observed on the steel surface, with a total oxide layer thickness of ∼ 114 μm. Martı́n et al.  [13]  immersed F82H steel in liquid LBE with an oxygen concentration of 8 × 10 -6  wt% at 600 ℃ for 500 h, and observed dissolution attack in local areas of the steel. The maximum penetration depth of PbBi into the steel matrix was ∼ 21 μm, and there was selective leaching of alloying elements. These findings demonstrate the strong corrosiveness of elevated-temperature liquid LBE on F/M steels. It poses significant safety concerns for reactor components, especially for thin-walled parts such as fuel cladding and heat exchanger tubes. Research has shown that the addition of Si element can significantly improve the corrosion resistance of F/M steels exposed to LBE  [14–18] . Recently, our group developed three F/M steels—12Cr-Y, 11Cr-1Si, and 11Cr-1Si-Y by using vacuum induction melting (VIM) combined with pre-laying Y powder at the bottom of the ingot mold  [19,20] . To evaluate their corrosion performance in liquid metal, the three steels were exposed to liquid LBE at 600 ℃ with an oxygen concentration of 10 -6  wt% for 2000 h  [21] . We found that 12Cr-Y with low Si content (0.2 wt%) suffered severe dissolution attack, and the maximum penetration depth of PbBi into the oxide scale was ∼ 30 μm. However, 11Cr-1Si and 11Cr-1Si-Y steels containing 1 wt% Si formed a dense Fe-Cr spinel oxide film, and no dissolution corrosion and the leaching of alloying elements was found on the steel surface. Further analysis for microstructure of the oxide layer revealed that Si addition promoted the formation of SiO 2  oxides in the Fe-Cr spinel layer. These SiO 2  particles acted as nucleation sites for Cr-rich oxides, accelerating the formation of a dense protective oxide film. Furthermore, Y segregation at the grain boundaries of 11Cr-1Si-Y steel hindered outward diffusion of the cations and promoted the nucleation of SiO 2  and Cr 2 O 3 , thereby obviously enhancing the corrosion resistance of 11Cr-1Si-Y.

However, the negative effect of adding Si element is due to its role as a ferrite forming element, which can lead to the precipitation of δ-ferrite in the steels  [22] . The nucleation of cracks at the δ-ferrite/martensite phase boundaries and their unimpeded propagation in the δ-ferrite phase are primary contributors to the reduced impact toughness of high-Si F/M steels  [23,24] . To mitigate the embrittlement of Si-containing steels caused by δ-ferrite phase, we developed 9Cr-1Si-Y steel by appropriately reducing the Cr content, aiming to achieve the required mechanical properties while maintaining enhanced corrosion resistance in liquid LBE. On the basis of developing this material, the fabrication of large-sized, small-diameter thin-walled tubes suitable for LFR has become another major challenge.

Fuel cladding tubes of LFR usually need to meet strict dimensions (outer diameter ≤ 10 mm, wall thickness ≤ 0.5 mm, length > 3000 mm) to ensure neutron economy and heat transfer efficiency  [25] . The addition of Si element in the steels increases the forming difficulty of the tubes. Currently, the primary method for manufacturing thin-walled tubes involves Pilger rolling combined with inter-pass annealing  [26,27] . Sun et al.  [28]  and Aghamiri et al.  [29]  have successfully fabricated FeCrAl alloy thin-walled tubes that meet the dimensional requirements for LFR application via the above process. Ge et al.  [30]  successfully prepared 12Cr-0.55Si steel tubes with a size of Φ12 × 0.8 mm through 4 passes of cold rolling and intermediate annealing. However, there are few reports on the processing technology and performance evaluation of high-Si F/M steel tubes. Another attention is that the cladding in LFR will serve at the temperatures above 600 ℃ for long periods, so the high-temperature mechanical properties of these tubes are directly related to reactor operational safety  [1,31] . Strain hardening behavior is a key indicator for characterizing the ability of steels to resist continuous deformation, thereby evaluating the high-temperature service stability of the material. Therefore, it is necessary to research the influence of processing technology on the microstructure and mechanical properties of 9Cr-1Si-Y thin-walled tubes.

In this study, high-Si F/M steel thin-walled tubes with an outer diameter of 5 mm, a wall thickness of 0.5 mm and a length of 3200 mm were fabricated via the process of 9-pass cold rolling with intermediate annealing and final normalizing and tempering treatments. The evolution of texture and microstructure during the process was characterized by various techniques. The mechanical properties and strain hardening mechanism of the finished tubes were analyzed through tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures. This work has a positive role for the process optimization and practical application of high-Si F/M steel cladding.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
The material here is high-Si F/M steel, and the nominal chemical composition is shown in  Table 1 
                         . Si (1 wt%) element was added to improve corrosion resistance, and small amounts of W, V, Ta, and Ti were used to provide solution and precipitation strengthening effects.

An ingot with a weight of 200 kg was prepared by vacuum induction melting (VIM) process. A combined process of N 2  backfilling in induction furnace after refining and nitrided ferrochrome alloy addition was adopted to achieve the target N content of 0.04 wt%. After complete melting of raw materials, the Ar pressure inside the furnace was adjusted to 70 kPa for refining for ∼ 15 min, followed by introducing N 2  (99.99%) to raise the pressure by 10 kPa upon refining completion. Nitrided ferrochrome alloy (N content: 0.06 wt%) was added into molten steel, and the melt was held at 1560–1590 °C for > 5 min to ensure full dissolution. Subsequently, pure Y blocks (Y content: 0.15 wt%) and Ti particles (Ti content: 0.03 wt%) were wrapped with thin iron sheets, and inserted directly below the molten steel surface via the feeding bin. The molten steel was held for 3 min and then poured immediately. The final recovery rates of N, Y and Ti in the ingots were ∼ 65%, ∼20% and ∼ 60%, respectively.

The ingot was forged into a round billet with a size of Φ220 mm × 500 mm at 1150–1200 ℃, and processed into a smooth bar with a final size of Φ204 mm × 450 mm for hot extrusion. A sample with a size of 20 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm was acquired from the forged billet. Then, the polished forged sample was chemically etched in a mixed solution of HF and HNO 3  (volume ratio 1:20, HF: 40%, HNO 3 : ≥65%) until the surface was slightly grey, followed by cleaning with ethanol.

The microstructure of the forged high-Si RAFM steel is presented in  Fig. 1 
                         . As shown in the OM and the EBSD figures ( Fig. 1 a, b), the forged steel exhibits a typical lath martensitic matrix with a small fraction of δ-ferrite (∼2.5%). The δ-ferrite appears as discrete islands within the martensitic matrix. Additionally, a small number of quadrilateral precipitates with a maximum size < 5 μm, denoted by green circles in  Fig. 1 a, are observed to be sparsely distributed in the microstructure. Further observations using SEM reveal a high density of nano-sized precipitates uniformly dispersed within the lath martensite ( Fig. 1 c). These precipitates appear bright white in BSE image. At higher magnification image ( Fig. 1 d), the nano-sized precipitates are clearly visible as fine spherical particles. EDS point analysis verifies that these bright nano-precipitates are (Ta, V)(C, N) carbonitrides (Spectrum 1,  Fig. 1 f). In contrast, the quadrilateral precipitates are clearly visible in  Fig. 1 e, and the corresponding EDS analysis identifies them as TiN particles (Spectrum 2,  Fig. 1 f).

sections.heading: Tube preparation process
paragraphs:
First, a through hole with a diameter of Φ80 mm was drilled axially in the center of the smooth bar with a size of Φ204 mm × 450 mm to obtain the hollow billet. Next, the hollow billet was heated to 1150 ℃ in a heating furnace for 4 h. Subsequently, the hot hollow billet was fed into the container of a hot extruder with a maximum force of 3500 t, and plastic deformation was realized under the combined action of the extrusion stem, extrusion die and mandrel. Hot extrusion can offset and reduce the damage to the billet caused by additional stress due to non-uniform deformation. By the intense triaxial stress, the coarse grains in the forged microstructure were transformed into equiaxed fine-grained structure, significantly improving the strength of pierced tube. Finally, the hot-extruded tube was subjected to straightening, refining, grinding, and shortening to obtain a bright tube with a diameter of 78 mm and a wall of 7 mm. The bright tube was processed into thin-walled tubes (designated T-Φ5) with final dimensions of Φ5 mm × 0.5 mm × 3200 mm through 9-pass cold rolling and intermediate annealing. The deformation and annealing parameter of each pass are shown in  Table 2 
                         . After the final cold rolling, the tube was normalized at 1050 ℃ for 10 min in a vertical furnace followed by argon cooling, and then tempered at 750 ℃ for 60 min followed by argon cooling. The heat-treated tube was degreased, pickled, and polished to obtain the finished tube (T-Φ5). T-Φ5 shows no visible cracks after flaring test (flaring ratio 30%) and flattening test (compressed to closure), confirming the excellent manufacturing quality.

sections.heading: Characterization and test methods
paragraphs:
Fig. 2 
                         a shows the microstructure characterization positions of T-Φ5. AD, TD, and RD represent the axial, transverse, and radial directions of the tube, respectively. The longitudinal section (AD-RD plane) is parallel to the AD, and the cross section (TD-RD plane) is perpendicular to the AD. The microstructure of the tube was observed using a scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi, Regulus 8100) equipped with secondary electron (SE) detector and backscattered electron detector (BSD). CR-3, AT-3, CR-6, AT-6, and T-Φ5 specimens were electropolished in a mixed solution of perchloric acid and ethanol (volume ratio 1:10) at −20 ℃ to remove the surface plastic deformation layer. The parameters were set as a voltage of 20 V and an current of 0.5–0.6 A. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) data were collected by an SEM equipped with an EBSD detector (Oxford Nordlysmax2) for tube texture analysis, and the AD-RD and TD-RD planes were characterized with a scanning step size of 0.4–0.5 μm. EBSD data were analyzed via AztecCrystal software to obtain grain boundary (GB), inverse pole figure (IPF), orientation distribution function (ODF). Thin foil specimens of the tube were prepared by mechanical thinning followed by ion milling for transmission electron microscopy (TEM, Tecnai F20, 200 kV) characterization. The morphology and crystal structure of precipitates were further analyzed via high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) and selected area electron diffraction (SAED).

Micro-Vickers hardness test was performed on the cross section of the tubes with a load of 200 gf and a holding time of 15 s. Seven parallel measurements were acquired as the final hardness value. To analyze the mechanical properties and strain hardening behavior of the tube, tensile tests were conducted on T-Φ5 tube at room temperature (RT), 200, 400, 500, 600, and 650 ℃ in accordance with GB/T 228.1–2021 and GB/T 228.2–2015 ( Fig. 2 b). Before the test, metal plugs were inserted into both ends of the tube to prevent the tube clamping section from sliding during tensile process. The room temperature tensile rate was set to 6.7 × 10 −3  s −1 , and the high-temperature tensile rate was 1.4 × 10 −3  s −1 . The total length of tensile sample was 170 mm at RT and 480 mm at high temperature. The gauge length of all specimens was 50 mm.

sections.heading: Texture evolution of high-Si F/M steel tubes during cold rolling and annealing
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          shows the EBSD maps, IPFs, and ODF sections of the high-Si F/M steel tube on the TD-RD and AD-RD planes after the 3rd cold rolling pass. Black lines represent high angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, >15°), while grey lines denote low angle grain boundaries (LAGBs, 2 ∼ 15°). CR-3 subjected to cold rolling with a 56.7% reduction exhibits a typical cold-deformed microstructure. Grains appear equiaxed in TD-RD plane, whereas the image on AD-RD plane reveals that grains severely elongated and fragmented along the rolling direction (i.e. AD), forming a continuous fiber/banded structure parallel to the AD ( Fig. 3 a and d). The high proportion of LAGB (67% and 85%) on the TD-RD and AD-RD planes suggests dislocation tangles and substructure induced by large plastic deformation in the tube. The substantial strain effectively drives the fragmentation of original grains and the formation of subgrains  [26,27] . Notably, the obvious color difference within individual grain further confirms localized changes in crystal orientation caused by cold rolling.

As confirmed by the IPFs in  Fig. 3 b and e, specific orientation textures formed in the CR-3 tube during cold rolling. Two main types of textures were observed on the TD-RD and AD-RD planes: α-fiber (<110>//AD) and γ-fiber (<111>//RD). These are consistent with the cold rolling deformation textures of BCC structure metals reported in the literatures  [32] . The texture components of BCC metals are typically characterized using ODF sections at φ2 = 45°. As shown in  Fig. 4 
                         a, CR-3 tube underwent recrystallization during annealing. Fiber/banded structures were largely replaced by recrystallized ferrite grains which exhibited clear and regular grain boundaries. Compared to cold-deformed grains, the internal defects of recrystallized grains were obviously reduced. However, there are still ∼ 15% of the grains that have not fully recrystallized, representing residual cold-rolled substructures ( Fig. 4 a and d). In fact, the cold-rolled tube was annealed at 800 ℃ for only 30 min, allowing most deformation-induced subgrains to complete the “nucleation-growth” process via recrystallization. The remaining subgrains failed to fully recrystallize due to insufficient local distortion energy or pinning effects from precipitates that hindered the migration of subgrain boundaries. The characteristic LAGBs in incompletely recrystallized grains reflect a transitional microstructure where recrystallized grains coexist with deformed substructures after the annealing. Notably, the recrystallized ferrite grains in the AD-RD plane are elongated along the AD, which may be related to the orientation of nucleation cores inheriting the preferred orientation of deformed subgrains. Meanwhile, grain growth along the RD may be constrained by the texture of the surrounding deformed matrix.  Fig. 4 b and e reveal that there are also α-fiber (<110>//AD) and γ-fiber (<111>//RD) textures in the AT-3 tube. ODF analysis indicates that the texture components in the recrystallized microstructure are more dispersed and the texture intensity is lower than that in the cold-rolled state ( Fig. 4 c and f).

Fig. 5 
                         a shows the EBSD morphology of CR-6 tube on the AD-RD plane. Grains in the CR-6 are elongated along the AD, exhibiting a banded structure similar to CR-3. LAGBs constitute 85% of all GBs, while HAGBs only account for 15%, which reflects that recrystallized grains formed after the 5th-pass annealing (AT-5) were transformed back into deformation subgrains during cold rolling. The cold rolling reduction in the 6th pass is only 39.7%, so the CR-6 sample has a larger grain width along the RD compared to CR-3. IPFs for the AD, TD, and RD reveal that the texture components of the cold-deformed grains are still α-fiber and γ-fiber. The maximum MUD of textures is 3.94, demonstrating a weakening compared to CR-3 ( Fig. 5 b).

As shown in  Fig. 5 c, the elongated banded microstructures in the CR-6 sample were replaced by equiaxed grains after annealing at 800 ℃ for 30 min. The proportion of LAGBs decreased to 58%, while that of HAGBs increased to 42%, which indicated that recrystallization occurred during the annealing. However, a fraction of deformed grains remains incompletely recrystallized, resulting in the retention of deformed substructures. IPFs show that the α-fiber texture formed by cold deformation was further transformed into γ-fiber texture during recrystallization ( Fig. 5 d). The proportion of LAGBs (58%) in the AT-6 sample is significantly higher than that in the AT-3 sample (47%). This is attributed to the CR-6 sample undergoing a lower cold rolling reduction (39.7%), which leads to relatively lower stored energy in the deformed microstructure and consequently a weaker driving force for recrystallization.

As shown in  Fig. 6 
                         , T-Φ5 tube shows typical lath martensite microstructure after final normalizing and tempering treatments, with no evidence of deformed subgrains from cold rolling and equiaxed ferrite grains formed during recrystallization ( Fig. 6 a and d). LAGBs account for 40% and HAGBs account for 60% in TD-RD plane. LAGBs correspond to martensite lath and block boundaries, while HAGBs correspond to martensite packet and prior austenite grain (PAG) boundaries. As shown in  Fig. 6 b and e, IPFs exhibit three types of textures: <110>//AD, <001>//RD, and < 111>//RD. sections.heading: Microstructure of the precipitates
paragraphs:
Fig. 7 
                          shows the precipitates morphologies in the T-Φ5 tube. A large number of fine precipitates are distributed at the PAG, martensite packet, block, and lath boundaries ( Fig. 7 a and b). Two types of precipitates can be clearly distinguished from the BSD image ( Fig. 7 b and c). EDS point analysis results further confirm that the grey rod-shaped particles (marked by green arrows) are rich in C and Cr elements (pt1), while the bright white spherical particles (marked by yellow arrows) have an enrichment of C, N, Ta, and V elements (pt2). Based on HAADF-STEM and SAED images, these two types of precipitates are identified as M 23 C 6  (M = Fe, Cr) carbides and MX (M = Ta, V; X=C, N) precipitates, as shown in  Fig. 8 
                          
                         [33] .

As shown in  Table 3 
                         , statistical analysis of the PAGs and precipitates in the T-Φ5 tube from five micrographs indicates that the average size of M 23 C 6  is 162.1 ± 59.7 nm, and that of MX precipitates is 42.8 ± 25.0 nm.  Fig. 9 
                          illustrates the size distribution of the PAGs. The histogram displays the distribution frequency across different grain size intervals, and the orange line represents the fitted curve. The PAG size of T-Φ5 ranges from 7.5 to 32.5 μm, with an average value of 17.3 ± 5.2 μm. The peak frequency is concentrated within the 10–20 μm interval.

sections.heading: Hardness of high-Si F/M steel tubes during cold rolling and annealing
paragraphs:
Fig. 10 
                          shows the hardness evolution of high-Si F/M steel from the forged state to the finished tube. The as-forged sample exhibits a hardness of 425 ± 5 HV 0.2 , while the hardness of CR-3 is 290 ± 3 HV 0.2 . Subsequent intermediate annealing induced recrystallization in the deformed structure, yielding soft ferritic grains. The hardness of AT-3 tube further decreased to 197 ± 6 HV 0.2 . During the 6th cold rolling pass, extensive dislocations were introduced into the recrystallized grains, resulting in structural hardening again. The hardness of CR-6 increased to 278 ± 4 HV 0.2 . The 6th-pass intermediate annealing repeats the recrystallization softening effect, with the hardness of the AT-6 tube decreasing to 190 ± 5 HV 0.2 . Ultimately, the microstructure of the T-Φ5 tube after normalizing and tempering is transformed into lath martensite with a consistent hardness of 264 ± 5 HV 0.2 .

sections.heading: Tensile properties of high-Si F/M steel tube
paragraphs:
Table 4 
                          show the tensile properties of the T-Φ5 tube at different temperatures. Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS) at RT reach 815 MPa and 686 MPa, respectively. Both UTS and YS gradually decreased with the growth of test temperature. These values declined to 279 MPa and 247 MPa at 650 ℃, respectively. However, total elongation (TE) displays an initial decrease followed by an increase with rising test temperature. TE decreased from 24.5% to 17.5% in the range of RT to 400 ℃, while progressively increased to 34.5% at 650 ℃. This phenomenon is mainly attributed to the effect of dynamic strain aging (DSA)  [34] . The diffusion rate of solution atoms in the steel increases with raising temperature, and they combine with moving dislocations to form Cottrell atmospheres that hinder dislocation slip, thereby leading to a decrease in elongation. When the temperature exceeds 400 ℃, dislocations achieve depinning through cross-slip and climb. The plastic deformation resistance of the steel is significantly reduced, resulting in an increase in elongation. Uniform elongation (UE) of the T-Φ5 tube continuously decreases with increasing test temperature, from 14.6% at RT to 1.0% at 650 ℃.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: In this work, high-Si F/M steel thin-walled tube was prepared via multi-pass cold rolling, intermediate annealing and final heat treatment. The evolution of textures, precipitates, and mechanical properties of the tube were systematically investigated. It is necessary to further discuss the strengthening mechanism and clarify the strain hardening behavior of the finished tube at different temperatures.

The essence is the dislocation tangles and dislocation walls formed in tempered martensite, which significantly increase the resistance to dislocation slip. Notably, the addition of Si element yields an obvious solid-solution strengthening effect in F/M steel. The addition of 1 wt% Si provides a solid-solution strengthening contribution of 83 MPa, which is remarkably higher than those of W and Mn elements. The dissolved Si atoms in the martensitic matrix increase lattice friction resistance and hinder dislocation slip. They also promote dislocation multiplication and entanglement during cold deformation  [37] . This leads to rapid work hardening and increased flow stress, and further raises the cold forming difficulty of small-diameter thin-walled tubes.

To reduce the high deformation resistance induced by Si and avoid tube cracking during cold rolling, a process of 9-pass cold rolling combined with intermediate annealing was used in this work. A relatively large reduction of 56.7%–69.7% was applied in the first three rolling passes. At this stage, the initial tube has a large wall thickness and can withstand heavy deformation, which rapidly reduces the tube size close to the target value. With the continuous thinning of tube wall, work hardening gradually accumulates in the material. Accordingly, the reduction of intermediate passes (CR-4 to CR-8) was decreased to 33.4%–40.4% to avoid local stress concentration and rolling cracking. The final pass adopts a small reduction of 18.5%, which ensures good surface quality, dimensional accuracy and straightness of the finished thin-walled tube.

                         where σ and ε represent the true stress and true strain in the tensile test. n = 1/m and k = 1/k′ denote the strain hardening exponent and strengthening coefficient. The strain hardening exponent is calculated by determining the slope of the ln(dσ/dε) vs. lnσ curves. As shown in  Fig. 12 
                         , the strain hardening curves of the T-Φ5 tube at different temperatures show obvious stage characteristics and temperature dependence. The period of different stages and the strain hardening exponent reflect the mechanism of dislocation motion, DSA, and dislocation recovery in the tube  [34,45,46] .

The strain hardening curve at RT exhibits distinct three-stage characteristic ( Fig. 12 a). In stage I, the ln(dσ/dε) decreases rapidly with increasing stress, which may be due to the uniform formation of dislocations in the lath martensite  [47] . When the dislocation density in the martensitic laths accumulates to a critical value, a large number of dislocations pile-up and entangle at the lath boundaries, leading to an increase of dislocation motion resistance. This causes the curve to flatten (stage II), corresponding to a strain hardening exponent n Ⅱ =0.256. Stage II is dominated by dislocation interaction which effectively delays the initiation of the necking stage. During the transition from stage II to stage III, the curve slope decreases sharply. This is driven by stress fields generated from dislocation pile-ups at lath boundaries, promoting dislocation propagation into adjacent laths. The rapid decay of strain hardening rate in stage III indicates localized stress concentration in the tube, implying the initiation of the necking stage.

However, the strain hardening curves at elevated temperatures exhibit clear differences compared to that at RT. Stage II gradually shortens with increasing test temperature until it disappears completely. The curve still remains the three-stage characteristic at 200 ℃. The dislocation multiplication mode corresponding to stage I is similar to that at RT, with dislocations forming uniformly within the martensite laths. Stage II is shorter than that at RT. This suggests that the stability of strain hardening decreases with increasing temperature, which is related to DSA effect. The diffusion rate of solution atoms in the steel increases with the growth of test temperature. The Cottrell atmospheres formed by the concentration of solution atoms around dislocations hinder dislocation slip, thereby delaying dislocation pile-ups and tangles at the lath boundaries  [34,47,48] . However, the interaction between solution atoms and dislocation remains relatively weak at 200 ℃. Dislocation pile-ups and tangles at the lath boundaries still exist in stage II. Stage III represents the process of dislocation expansion to adjacent laths. TE of the tube decreases from 24.5% for RT to 22.5% for 200 ℃, and UE significantly dropped to 6.1%, characterized by reduced strain hardening stability and diminished plasticity ( Table 4 ).

When the test temperature reaches 400 ℃, the interaction between solution atoms and dislocation dominated by DSA is substantially enhanced. Stage I on the ln(dσ/dε) vs. lnσ curve is flatter than that at RT and 200 ℃, corresponding to a higher strain hardening exponent (n I  = 0.071). At this point, the diffusion rate of solution atoms matches the rate of dislocation glide optimally, with the Cottrell atmosphere impeding dislocation motion in the laths at the initial stage of deformation. The strain hardening exponent in Stage II increases compared to that at 200 ℃. This is primarily due to the weakening influence of interstitial C and N atoms on DSA, while substitutional Cr and Si atoms dominated the DSA effect at 400 ℃  [48] . Dislocation motion displays a burst-like growth characteristic of “pinning-depinning-repinning”. The discontinuous dislocation motion destroys the condition of stable hardening and exacerbates deformation inhomogeneity, finally resulting in the premature local stress concentration. Consequently, UE of the tube decreased to 3.7%, and TE dropped to a trough value of 17.5% at 400 ℃. At 500 ℃, the DSA effect weakens and dynamic recovery of dislocation gradually occurs, reducing dislocation pile-up effects at lath boundaries  [34,47,49] . This caused a sharp decline in the strain hardening capacity of the tube, manifested as stage II approaching disappearance and a UE of 3.0%. However, due to the recovery of plastic deformation in the necking area, TE of the tube has increased to 28.0% at 500 ℃, and the mechanical properties show a trend of strength decrease but plastic recovery.

At elevated temperatures of 600 and 650 ℃, the strain hardening curves exhibit consistent characteristics. The stable hardening stage (stage II) has completely disappeared, retaining only the initial hardening stage (stage I) and the pre-necking hardening stage (stage III). The strain hardening rate during the initial hardening stage remains constantly low. In stage III, the strain hardening rate decreases sharply, indicating the rapid initiation and development of necking. The accelerated decrease in strain hardening rate at elevated temperatures is attributed to the significant increase in thermal activation energy, which promotes the dynamic balance between dislocation multiplication and annihilation during tensile deformation. Consequently, the dislocation density in the martensitic laths remains low and hinders the formation of stable interactions such as pile-ups and tangles. Simultaneously, dislocations are rearranged through climb and cross-slip, and their motion resistance is substantially weakened  [34,47,50] . The weakened strain hardening effect makes the deformation of the tube quickly concentrate in the necking region, manifested as the low UE (only 1.0%) at 650 ℃.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
In this study, a thin-walled tube with small diameter (T-Φ5) was fabricated via 9-pass cold rolling and annealing combined with final normalizing and tempering treatments. The microstructure, texture, mechanical properties, and strain hardening behavior of the tube were systematically characterized and analyzed. The main conclusions are as follows: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Cold rolling leaded to the formation of elongated subgrains along the AD of the tube, accompanied by typical α-fiber (<110>//AD) and γ-fiber (<111>//RD) textures. These subgrains underwent recrystallization during intermediate annealing and transformed into equiaxed ferrite grains. The finished tube after normalizing and tempering exhibits a fully lath martensite microstructure. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            The PAG size of the T-Φ5 tube was 17.3 ± 5.2 μm, and two types of precipitates were observed in the microstructure of tube: M 23 C 6  carbides with an average size of 162.1 ± 59.7 nm distributed along PAG, martensitic packet, block, and lath boundaries; and MX precipitates with a mean size of 42.8 ± 25.0 which dispersed within the martensite laths. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            UTS and YS of the T-Φ5 tube at RT are 815 MPa and 686 MPa, respectively. These values decreased with the growth of test temperature, declining to 279 MPa and 247 MPa at 650 ℃. TE shows a variation of “first decrease and followed by increase” with a trough value of TE (17.5% at 400 ℃) dominated by DSA. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The strain hardening behavior of the T-Φ5 tube exhibits clear temperature dependence. UE of T-Φ5 tube at RT is 14.6%, primarily attributed to the stable stage (stage II) formed by dislocation pile-ups and tangles at martensitic lath boundaries. In the temperature range of 200–400 ℃, the strain hardening mechanism of the tube was affected by DSA, which significantly reduced the duration of stage II. When the test temperature exceeded 500 ℃, the dislocation recovery mechanism in the laths becomes dominant, and the strain hardening ability of the tube decreases sharply, resulting in low UE (1.0%) at 650 ℃.
